Wiring cheatsheet

Every pin, wire colour, baud rate, register and voltage in the toolkit, on one page. Written to be read on a phone with a probe in your other hand, and to print onto two sheets you can tape inside the enclosure lid.

Pin budget The two buses Wire colours Grounding Voltages Network Bring-up order Symptom → cause

1 · The pin budget

A NodeMCU 1.0 gives you five GPIOs that are both free and safe, and a combined node spends every one of them. There is no sixth. Plan around this before you design anything.

Every GPIO on a NodeMCU 1.0, and what it can actually be used for
PinGPIOUsed forWhy not
D1 GPIO5 safe Module 2 soil TX · farm-node water TX · water-level.ino DE
D2 GPIO4 safe valve relay IN
D5 GPIO14 safe Module 1 water RX · deep-sleep soil TX
D6 GPIO12 safe Module 1 water TX · deep-sleep soil RX
D7 GPIO13 safe Module 2 soil RX · farm-node water RX
D0 GPIO16 trap deep-sleep wake only No interrupts at all — it physically cannot receive SoftwareSerial.
D3 GPIO0 trap leave alone Boot strap — must be HIGH at boot.
D4 GPIO2 trap leave alone Boot strap — must be HIGH at boot.
D8 GPIO15 trap leave alone Boot strap — must be LOW at boot.
Worth knowing

This is why the toolkit standardises which pins each module claims. Wire Module 1 to D5/D6 and Module 2 to D7/D1 whether or not you build the other one — then if you later put both sensors on one board they simply coexist, with no rewiring and no thinking about it.

This will bite you

A bus has more than one correct pin assignment, and mixing them up gives you two dead buses. Ian's deployed farm-node runs water on D7/D1 — swapped relative to the standalone Module 1 build — because the board was soldered that way on 2026-07-19 and the firmware was made to follow the iron. The flashed binary is always authoritative. Every pin table below therefore names the .ino it was read out of; wire the one marked wire this one unless you are rebuilding our node specifically.

2 · The two RS485 buses

Two separate buses, one transceiver each — never one shared bus. Both probes ship as slave address 1 and run different bauds, so sharing would require writing address and baud registers on sensors we own exactly one of each. A second one-dollar transceiver deletes both problems and needs zero register writes.

0x0000 Moisture ÷10 → % unsigned

Watch out

Both values are signed int16 where marked. 0xFF9B is −10.1 °C, not 65435, and a water reading slightly below zero is real and legitimate. Parse into int16_t or your first frosty morning produces nonsense.

Worth knowing

Reads are safe; blind writes are not. Reading a register cannot damage a probe. Writing one you have not confirmed can land on its slave address or baud rate and cost you the ability to talk to the thing at all. Never write a register to “fix” a reading.

3 · Wire colours — the trap

The two probes use the same two colours for A and B, and they mean opposite things. Different manufacturers, no standard. This is the single easiest wiring mistake in the whole build, and it is most likely to catch you on the day you build the second module from muscle memory.

QDY30A — water

Blue = A+

Yellow = B−

Red = 18 V, green = ground

≠

THC-S — soil

Yellow = A+

Blue = B−

Brown = 4.5–30 V, black = ground

Worth knowing

Swapping A and B is harmless. If a probe never answers, swap the two data wires and try again before suspecting anything else. The TXD and RXD LEDs on the RS485 board are a free logic analyser: TXD flashes when the ESP asks, RXD flashes when the probe answers. TXD only means the probe isn't replying.

4 · Grounding — what must be common, and what must not

One ground for the sensing side. These are all the same electrical node:

probe green (water) ── MT3608 OUT− ── MT3608 IN− ── RS485 #1 GND ── RS485 #2 GND
      ── ESP GND ── probe black (soil) ── pack P−

The water probe runs on the boosted 18 V rail while the ESP runs on 3.3 V — two supplies, one shared return. Random intermittent failures with wiring that “looks right” are usually this.

Deliberately not common: when you bench the valve from a separate 12 V mains adapter, the solenoid draws through the relay's isolated switched contacts. Its current never touches USB and no common ground is wanted between the 12 V side and your laptop. That isolation is exactly why 12 V cannot backfeed the laptop.

This will bite you

Every load taps pack+ / P−, never B−. Tapping B− routes discharge around the BMS protection FETs and you lose over-discharge and short-circuit protection silently.

6 · Network

MethodPathPayload
uplink POST /water {node, ok, raw, depth_mm, valve, rssi, uptime_s}
uplink POST /soil {node, ok, moisture_pct, temp_c, ec, valve, rssi, uptime_s}
downlink GET (poll, 1 s) /valve "1" / "0"
page GET /page live readings, one card per node
page POST /valve/set sets flow.valveCmd
This will bite you

Leave POST_HOST empty. The phone running the hotspot is the node's gateway by definition. Android randomises the hotspot subnet — ours came up on 10.215.63.55, not the 192.168.43.1 every guide quotes — and a hardcoded IP goes stale silently: the node keeps reading perfectly and publishes into the void.

Watch out

Every http in node needs a paired http response, or the ESP blocks until timeout and reports a network fault that isn't one.

7 · Bring-up order

Not arbitrary. A panel has no off switch, and a boost converter set wrong destroys a probe.

  1. Cover the panel. Connect the battery through the BMS to the MPPT output, then uncover. Teardown is the reverse — cover and disconnect PV first, then the battery.
  2. Set the MT3608 to 18 V with nothing on its output. Meter it. Only then connect the probe's red wire.
  3. Verify one ground with a continuity beep: probe green ↔ ESP GND ↔ P−.
  4. Flash with BENCH_MODE 1 and prove both probes over serial, before WiFi joins the list of things that can be broken.
  5. Set BENCH_MODE 0; confirm serial prints a gateway : matching the phone, and POST /water: 200 ok.
  6. Curl the endpoint from a laptop before ever blaming firmware.
  7. Valve last, and only after its pull-in voltage is known.
# always compile --upload — a bare `upload` flashes a stale .bin
arduino-cli compile --upload --fqbn esp8266:esp8266:nodemcuv2 -p /dev/ttyUSB0 firmware/farm-node

# prove a probe from a laptop, before any ESP8266 exists
bun tools/poll-soil.ts  [device] [--once]     # THC-S, 4800 8N1
bun tools/poll-water.ts [device] [--once]     # QDY30A, 9600 8N1

# prove the base station, before blaming firmware
curl -X POST http://<phone-ip>:1880/water -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"node":"water-tank-1","ok":true,"depth_mm":500}'
Watch out

Do not use mbpoll with the cheap FT232 USB-RS485 adapter. It reports Invalid CRC on every frame while the sensor is perfectly fine — the adapter echoes your transmitted bytes back and mbpoll reads and writes on one file descriptor. The bundled bun pollers resync on a valid frame header and validate CRC properly.

8 · Symptom → cause

Every fault table in the toolkit, merged. If something is not working, start here.

SymptomAlmost alwaysWhat to do
No reading at all · Water tank level A and B swapped Swap the blue and yellow wires. This is common — try it before anything else.
No reading, probe cold · Water tank level Not enough voltage Meter red to green: it must read 18 V, not the raw battery.
Boost converter reads 0 V · Water tank level Trimmer parked mid-range It is 25-turn with no end stops. Keep turning, watch the meter.
Readings 10× off · Water tank level Wrong scaling 1 count = 1 mm. Check you are not treating it as centimetres.
Reading is about 65000 · Water tank level Read as unsigned It is signed int16. Readings slightly below zero are real and legitimate.
Reading never changes · Water tank level Wrong register It is 0x0004.
Readings fail randomly · Water tank level No common ground Probe green, boost OUT−, MAX485 GND and ESP GND must be one rail.
Drifts with the weather · Water tank level Breather tube blocked or wet Keep the loose cable end dry and open to air.
Reads, then silent, then reads · Water tank level The open intermittent A wire. Wiggle-test each one while the node polls, prime suspect green/ground. Do this before soldering.
No reading at all · Soil + irrigation valve A and B swapped Swap the yellow and blue wires — note these are opposite to Module 1.
No reading at all · Soil + irrigation valve Wrong baud This probe is 4800. Module 1's is 9600. Don't copy the number across.
Invalid CRC on every frame with mbpoll · Soil + irrigation valve Adapter echo, not a fault Use bun tools/poll-soil.ts. The sensor is fine.
modbus exception 0x01 · Soil + irrigation valve Used 0x30 from the manual The manual has a typo. The function code is 0x03.
Temperature reads ~65000 · Soil + irrigation valve Parsed as unsigned Cast to int16_t. 0xFF9B = −10.1 °C.
Moisture always 0 and the probe IS buried · Soil + irrigation valve Air gap around the tines Pack the soil firmly against the probe.
Relay clicks but the valve doesn't move · Soil + irrigation valve Not enough volts at the coil under load Meter across the valve while the relay is on. A sagging pack meters fine at rest.
Relay doesn't click at all · Soil + irrigation valve Powered from VIN Use VBUS. VIN floats when the board is on USB.
ESP reboots when the valve closes · Soil + irrigation valve Missing flyback diode Fit the 1N5819 across the valve terminals, stripe to +.
Valve chatters on and off · Soil + irrigation valve Thresholds too close Leave ≥10 points between dry and wet.
Valve never closes · Soil + irrigation valve Water isn't reaching the probe Blocked dripper, empty tank, kinked line. Your max run time should have caught this — if it didn't, fix that first.
Valve opens on a full battery, not a flat one · Soil + irrigation valve Solenoid under-volted See the open question on valve power.
Valve energised, nothing flows · Soil + irrigation valve Below the valve's minimum pressure differential A pilot valve needs ~0.2 bar. Check the head above it; if marginal, spec a direct-acting “0 bar” valve.
No output voltage · Solar power Fuse has blown Check and replace it — then find out why.
Pack charges partway then stops, never reaches full · Solar power Panel Vmp too low once hot Subtract ~11% from the label Vmp and check it is ≳2 V above the pack's full-charge voltage.
Charges fine in the morning, stops by midday · Solar power Same cause — the panel heated up and Vmp fell Higher-Vmp panel, or fewer cells in series.
Panel gives far less current than its rating · Solar power Facing the wrong way In the southern hemisphere the midday sun is in the NORTH. Check Voc and Isc disconnected to confirm the panel itself is healthy.
BMS cuts power suddenly · Solar power A cell is faulty or badly connected Check every connection, test each cell individually.
Phone charges very slowly — looks like the panel is too small · Solar power USB data pins not shorted Short D+ to D− at the socket. Confirm with a USB power meter that it now draws >0.5 A. This failure impersonates a solar problem.
Phone charges but never reaches full on a sunny day · Solar power Voltage drop in a long thin USB cable at 2 A Shorter, thicker cable; set the buck to 5.15–5.2 V.
Enclosure gets very hot inside · Solar power No ventilation Vent holes on the shaded side, meshed to keep bugs out.
Node can't find the WiFi network · Base station Hotspot off, or name mismatch Check the hotspot is on and the SSID matches config.h exactly.
Can't open Node-RED in the browser · Base station Node-RED isn't running Open Termux and start it again — and check the wake-lock.
Dashboard shows no data · Base station Node posting to the wrong address Leave POST_HOST empty and let the node derive it from the gateway.
Flow looks healthy but nothing is scheduled · Base station Android froze the timer Make it event-driven; hold a wake-lock; set Termux to Unrestricted.
Phone battery drains fast · Base station Hotspot + Node-RED never sleep Keep it charged — and on solar, duty-cycle the charger, not the phone.
Mobile data disappearing quickly · Base station Sending too often Batch readings, or send summaries rather than every sample.

Generated from the same data as the module pages — the pin maps come from firmware/farm-node/farm-node.ino, the power figures from hardware/3S2P.md, and the endpoints from the Node-RED flows. If a table here disagrees with the hardware, the hardware is right and this page is a bug: open an issue.

Farmers IoT Toolkit

An open-source toolkit that shows farmers how to build low-cost IoT sensors on ESP8266 microcontrollers. Four modules, full parts lists, and honest build guides that say what is proven and what is not.

Open source — use, share, and adapt freely.
